extracted.intended_audience: theatre practitioners, performers, students of aesthetics, and scholars of Indian classical art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing or evaluating dramatic performances that aim to evoke Bharata's concept of Rasa by mobilizing determinants (Vibhava), consequents (Anubhava), transitory states (Vyabhicari Bhava), and the stable Sthayibhava, while attending to audience receptivity (Sahridaya).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goal of performance: evoke Rasa
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary goal of performance in Bharata's framework is not mere entertainment but to transport the audience into a parallel reality where they taste Natyarasa and can reflect on moral, spiritual, and emotional truths. (“na hi Rasad rite kaschid arthah pravartate” – no meaningful idea can be conveyed if Rasa is not evoked.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entertainment is possible but secondary; a performance without evoked Rasa is considered artless. Design all elements (text, acting, music, stagecraft) to serve the evocation and intensification of Rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa as aesthetic essence, not literal emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa denotes the essence or 'aesthetic relish' of an emotional experience — a transformed, aesthetically elevated form of emotion that the spectator tastes rather than the raw personal emotion of actor or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate actor's private feeling with Rasa. Structure performance so the audience (Sahridaya) can 'taste' the essence: distance and awareness (spectator knows it's performance) are part of Natya Rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa Sutra (production formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is produced from the combination of Vibhava (determinants), Anubhava (consequents), and Vyabhicari Bhavas (transitory psychological states) in conjunction with the Sthayibhava: 'Vibhava–anubhava-vyabhichari-samyogad rasa nishpattih.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create Rasa, ensure all three element-classes are present and interact to intensify a Sthayibhava. The sutra functions as the central organizing principle for composing emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vibhava (determinants) — alambana and uddipana
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibhava refers to the stimulating cause or external circumstance that triggers emotion. Bharata identifies two types: Alambana Vibhava (primary, foundational stimulus like the hero/heroine) and Uddipana Vibhava (environmental/supporting stimuli that intensify the emotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing scenes, clearly establish Alambana elements that provide emotional basis, and deploy Uddipana cues (lighting, setting, props, weather, music) to amplify and deepen the felt mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anubhava (consequents / physical expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anubhava is the outward, physical manifestation through which an actor communicates inner emotional state — e.g., weeping, trembling voice, drooping limbs for sorrow; burning eyes, heaving chest for anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anubhava encompasses speech (vachika), physical gesture (angika), and inner sincerity (sattvika). Bharata prescribes detailed physical expressions so the spectator immediately recognizes and connects with the intended emotion; gestures should be specific and legible to the Sahridaya.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vyabhicari Bhava (transitory companion states)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vyabhicari Bhavas (also called Sanchari Bhavas) are the transitory, complementary psychological states (Bharata lists 33) that weave in and out of performance, enriching and intensifying the dominant emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fleeting states—apprehension, exhaustion, intoxication, pride, etc.—to colour scenes dynamically. They must support, not supplant, the dominant Sthayibhava; their mobility (vyabhichari = 'to move') sustains variation and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sthayibhava (stable emotional core)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sthayibhava is the stable, dominant emotional state that persists throughout a performance and, when heightened by other elements, transforms into Rasa. Bharata identifies eight Sthayibhavas (Rati, Hasa, Shoka, Krodha, Utsaha, Bhaya, Jugupsa, Vismaya).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the drama in a sustained emotional key: select a Sthayibhava to function as the work's emotional bedrock, and ensure Vibhava, Anubhava, and Vyabhicari Bhavas consistently intensify and generalize that state toward universalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: The (original) eight Rasas and their correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata articulated eight Rasas—Shringara (erotic), Hasya (comic), Karuna (compassionate), Raudra (furious), Veera (heroic), Bhayanaka (terrible), Bibhatsa (odious), Adbhuta (wondrous)—each mapped to a Sthayibhava, presiding deity, and symbolic colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming at a particular Rasa, attend to its traditional correspondences (symbol, deity, colour) as organizing motifs. Note later addition of Shanta (peaceful/tranquil) as a ninth Rasa in subsequent aesthetics (Abhinavagupta).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natya Rasa: aesthetic distance and collective sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Natya Rasa is distinct from real-life emotion: although spectator and actor know the situation is not literally real, they are nevertheless moved; the experience is simultaneously real and distanced, and it is collectively shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a shared emotional atmosphere onstage that invites spontaneous audience participation (weeping, laughter) without misleading literal belief. The actor acts as 'bearer, medium, and connector' of the character's emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sattvika Bhavas (involuntary responses) as markers of authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sattvika Bhavas are involuntary physiological responses—trembling, perspiration, tears, change in voice, fainting—considered the most authentic markers of genuine emotional depth in performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize inner identification over surface mimicry so involuntary signs of feeling can arise; training should aim for sincere affective embodiment rather than merely technical gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor's role: embodying Bhavas to open emotional world
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor is described as the bearer and connector of the character’s emotions; by embodying the Bhavas on stage, the actor progressively opens the character's emotional world and draws the audience into it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting technique should focus on credible embodiment of Sthayibhava and its attendant Bhavas, making the inner life perceivable through calibrated Anubhava and Sattvika manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience receptivity: the Sahridaya requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is 'tasted' by a Sahridaya — a spectator who brings genuine emotional openness and aesthetic sensitivity; the quality of aesthetic experience thus depends on the audience as much as the performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that evocation of Rasa presupposes receptive spectatorship; staging, cultural codes, and communicative clarity should account for the intended audience's capacity to respond as Sahridayas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered psychological model: integrated system of 49 emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata's model classifies inner life into stable (8 Sthayibhavas), transitory (33 Vyabhicari Bhavas), and involuntary (8 Sattvika Bhavas) states — a total of 49 emotions that work in concert to produce Rasa rather than a simplistic actor→audience causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a layered, dynamic approach when crafting performances: coordinate causes, effects, transitory states, and dominant moods so they interact in calibrated ways, acknowledging complexity rather than linear mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-medium and tradition-specific application
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata's Rasa-Bhava framework underlies many classical Indian performing arts and has analogues in music (raga aiming to evoke mood) and in other cultural traditions influenced by Hindu aesthetics (e.g., Indonesian Ramayana performances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting Rasa theory to other media (cinema, digital) or cultural contexts, respect the framework's emphasis on combined determinants/consequents/transitory states while translating embodied and ritual conventions appropriately.
